Helmet Detection AI: every rider checked, from a phone video or a CCTV camera

An end-to-end system from Axom AI that finds each motorcycle rider, decides helmet or no helmet, and sends a photo alert for every rider without one.

  • CCTV cameras
  • Android app
  • Telegram alerts
  • No GPU needed
  • Open source

Quick answer

Helmet detection is computer vision that finds motorcycle riders and decides, person by person, whether a helmet is worn. Axom AI's system does this on uploaded videos and on live CCTV streams. On traffic-camera footage it had never seen, it caught about 74% of bare-headed riders when analysing one frame per second and about 90% at two frames per second, with about 1% of alerts on fully helmeted bikes. It runs on a normal CPU, with no GPU.

Why helmet detection matters

WHO reports that head trauma is the leading cause of death for motorcycle riders, and that safe, quality helmets reduce the risk of death by more than six times and the risk of brain injury by up to 74%. (World Health Organization, 2023). A helmet only helps when it is worn, and no team can watch every road.

Cameras already watch many junctions and highways. An AI model can read those streams all day, point at the riders without a helmet, and hand a human a photo to review. That is the idea behind this work: use the cameras that exist, and let people spend their time on the cases that matter.

What Axom AI built

Video analysis

Record or upload a clip in the Android app. The server finds every person, gives each one a single verdict and returns a photo with the time it was seen.

Live CCTV monitoring

A worker reads the RTSP stream of a camera, tracks every rider separately and raises one alert per person without a helmet. See CCTV monitoring.

Admin dashboard

Statistics, violation review, false-positive marking, camera management and a CCTV events page.

Alerts where people look

Telegram, the dashboard and an Alerts tab in the app, plus a warning when the monitor itself stops.

A retraining loop

Reviewers flag wrong detections; those frames become training data for the next version.

See it work

On a busy junction every rider gets their own verdict, so a bike with two people gives two results, not one (see the picture at the top of this page).

How it works in eight steps

  1. Take the picture. A phone video, or frames from a camera's RTSP stream.
  2. Find motorcycles. A general-purpose YOLOv8s model (trained on COCO) marks every motorcycle and bicycle.
  3. Find heads. Our fine-tuned YOLOv8s looks at the whole frame and, regularly, at an enlarged crop around each motorcycle, where small, far-away heads become big enough to judge.
  4. Decide helmet or no helmet. The detector gives a verdict; a small classifier looks at the head crop and can overrule it when it is very sure. Caps, hats and scarves count as no helmet.
  5. Keep only riders. A head must sit on a motorcycle and be a believable size. Pedestrians and cyclists have no helmet rule here, so they are ignored.
  6. Track every rider. Each head gets its own track, so one frame with many riders gives many verdicts.
  7. Confirm. A rider is flagged after one very sure sighting, or two sightings, without a helmet.
  8. Alert once. One photo with every rider boxed, a Telegram message, a dashboard event and an app alert; repeats of the same person are suppressed.

The full explanation, with the reasons behind each choice, is on How helmet detection works, from A to Z.

What we used

  • Ultralytics YOLOv8s
  • COCO-pretrained YOLOv8s
  • YOLOv8n-cls (crop classifier)
  • ByteTrack, then a custom tracker
  • OpenCV
  • PyTorch
  • FastAPI
  • PostgreSQL
  • Flutter and Dart
  • ONNX Runtime
  • Telegram Bot API
  • MediaMTX and FFmpeg (test camera)
  • Google Colab (T4 GPU)
  • nginx and Cloudflare
  • AWS Lightsail
  • HELMET dataset (CC BY 4.0)
  • Seven public Roboflow datasets

Honest limits

Night

The training data is daytime. On the same frames made to look like night, recall fell from 0.76 to 0.34. Night-style training images are prepared but the model has not been trained on them yet, and real night footage is still needed.

Distance

Heads that are only a few pixels wide are missed. Enlarged crops help; they cost speed.

Speed decides recall

The more frames analysed per second, the more riders are caught. A desktop CPU manages about 1.4.

Your camera is not ours

Our test footage is from Myanmar traffic cameras. Angle, light and clothing at your site will differ, and results will too.

A screening tool, not a judge

A person should review an alert before any action is taken against anyone.

Frequently asked questions

What is helmet detection?

Helmet detection is a computer vision task: a model looks at a photo, video or camera stream, finds each motorcycle rider and decides whether that person is wearing a helmet. Axom AI's system also saves a photo for every rider without a helmet.

How accurate is Axom AI helmet detection?

On held-out traffic-camera footage the live system caught about 74% of bare-headed riders when it analysed one frame per second and about 90% at two frames per second, with roughly 1% of alerts landing on fully helmeted bikes. After CCTV fine-tuning, recall on held-out frames rose from 0.62 to 0.79.

Does it work on CCTV cameras?

Yes. A worker program reads the camera's RTSP stream, tracks every rider separately and sends a photo alert to Telegram, the admin dashboard and the Axom AI Android app for each rider without a helmet.

Does it need a GPU?

No. The whole pipeline runs on a desktop CPU (an Intel Core i3) at about 1.4 analysed frames per second. A faster CPU or a GPU analyses more frames per second, which catches more riders.

Is the helmet detection code open source?

Yes. The backend and the Android app are published on GitHub under the MIT licence. The model builds on Ultralytics YOLOv8 (AGPL-3.0) and public datasets released under CC BY 4.0 and MIT, so check those terms before commercial use.
